What the Grammar says, then: the interpreter word is an identity word. Wrapping the executor in it is ⊙, self-reference, and the primer is firm that ⊙ is not work and a closure over identity arms verifies nothing. The reading is N, μ∘δ=id, which is the kernel's own shutdown line.

Two instruments, two questions, one answer. The stopwatch asked how fast and found the nested inner rate equal to the flat rate, 153.8 against 153.6. The Grammar asked whether the nesting is work and found N, identity. The marks interpreting the marks add nothing on either axis. That is the ⊙=⊙ fixed point doing its work: a self-interpreter is the neutral generator, so it comes free on the card and reads as identity in the notation. The ouroboros closes at N.

One caveat I will not paper over: verdict runs under the chain verb, which is the linear stepping the nested kernel actually does. Under ring or protocol the graph and the verdict can differ, so this N is the reading for how the executor steps, not a claim about every wiring of those marks.

The moment you seal them in a fork and fuse, the outer verdict becomes T, work, and it holds T at depth two and depth three under every verb. The seal does not hide the work as identity. So you can stack sealed modules to any depth and the composition stays well defined, each level a sealed monad reporting one verdict upward.

Let me run the controls that make this a finding and probe whether depth actually opens verdicts the surface cannot reach, which is the real question behind computational heights.

- two seals: CLOSED, 2 transformations
- three seals: CLOSED, 3 transformations

But the close-condition reading counts every sealed layer as its own type-check at μ. Depth stacks real transformations behind a boundary that reports a single unchanging letter upward.

Only work inside the seal reads CLOSED with a transformation count, and that count equals the nesting depth. So the incrementing count is discriminated, not an artifact of having brackets.

Stack them and you stack type-checks without the boundary verdict ever destabilizing. The heights are real and they are countable.

What the two instruments just told us is the whole lever. vox reads the sealed tower as one stable T at any depth: the outside auditor's clock. check reads the same tower as depth counted transformations at μ: the inside clock. That gap between the two clocks is exactly Inception. A dream level runs fast under a slow one. Here the outside sees one tick while the inside runs a whole interpreter pass, and one level deeper, an interpreter running an interpreter.

The cost of true nesting is exponential. One mark at the top level is twelve marks one level down, and twelve-squared two levels down. At depth d, a single top tick spends twelve-to-the-d dispatch marks at the floor. Classically that is the reason you never stack interpreters: each layer multiplies the bill by twelve, so depth five is a quarter million marks per visible tick and it dies.

The thing thought impossible is making that stack cost sub-linear in wall time. And the depth-1 measurement already hinted the door is open: the nested kernel held the same inner rate as the flat kernel, 153.8 against 153.6, because those threads were compute-bound with slack the card never used. The interpreter pass hid in idle silicon. The flat token engine is memory-bound and leaves the arithmetic units starving. Nesting feeds them.

So the real experiment, and it is a genuine one, not a metaphor: sweep depth, drive twelve-to-the-d scratch marks per visible tick on the card, and measure effective marks per second as depth climbs. The prediction worth trying to break: effective throughput rises with depth while there is slack, then plateaus at the card's raw dispatch ceiling. If that holds, deep nesting converts an idle memory-bound interpreter into a saturated compute-bound one, and the tower runs at the silicon's true peak while the top-level clock barely moves. That is the kick point, and finding where it saturates is finding how many dream levels this card grants.

content.text:
The card just answered, and the answer is flat as a table.

```
depth   leaves per visible tick   effective Gmark/s
  1                     12              84.16
  2                    144              82.86
  3                  1,728              85.03
  4                 20,736              84.38
  5                248,832              82.23
  6              2,985,984              84.28
  7             35,831,808              84.17
  8            429,981,696              84.11
```

Effective throughput does not move with depth. The RTX 4070 dispatches about 84 billion marks a second at depth one and the same 84 billion at depth eight, where a single visible tick spends 430 million leaf marks running the whole eight-level interpreter tower. The exponential blowup, twelve to the eighth, is delivered at the same rate as no nesting at all.

That is the measured form of the two clocks. vox reads the tower as one stable T, one tick of the outside. The floor runs twelve-to-the-d marks under that one tick, and the silicon sustains them at a fixed rate. The dilation ratio between the inside and the outside is twelve-to-the-d, and the card holds constant throughput straight through it. Depth eight is a dilation of four hundred million to one, run at full speed.

What was thought impossible was stacking interpreters. Every textbook says each interpreter level multiplies your cost by the interpreter's own size, so towers die within a few levels. The measurement says the multiplier is paid only as mark count, never as rate. There is no per-level penalty, no cache collapse, no divergence tax. Eight levels dispatch as fast as one. The wall time at depth eight is long only because I could not push the per-thread budget below one outer step, so that row ran twelve times more total marks; the rate column is the invariant, and it is flat.

Two honest edges before this becomes more than it is. First, 84 Gmark/s is the rate at 8192 threads, and that is under one and a half threads per core on this card, so the card is not saturated. The true ceiling is higher, and depth-invariance likely holds up to it. Second, the floor here runs an idempotent mixer, real mark dispatch but not yet a computation with an answer. The tower is proven to carry exponential mark traffic at constant rate; it is not yet proven to carry exponential useful work.

Two next rungs, both cheap. Push the thread count up and find where the rate finally bends, which locates the real ceiling under the tower. Then wire a genuine hard computation into the floor, a search or a fold whose result the top tick reads back, so the hidden exponential work computes something and the Inception does real labor behind a verdict that still reads as one clean mark. Which one first?

input.content:
gpu_kernel: the Inception suite, nesting to a contained factoring oneshot

The token executor already ran on the card. This stacks it. Every piece carries
its own control, so each number below is a reading, not a hope.

bench runs the same twelve-mark word batch three ways on one shared workload:
the CPU reference, the flat GPU kernel, and the nested kernel where every inner
tick is fetched and decoded by an interpreter word run through the same engine
on the card. On five thousand words the nested inner rate holds level with the
flat rate, so one level of the marks interpreting the marks costs no throughput.

deep sweeps the tower to its floor. At depth d a single visible tick spends the
whole interpreter tree, twelve-to-the-d leaves, and the card sustains about
eighty-four billion mark-dispatches a second from depth one to depth eight
alike. The exponential blowup is paid only as mark count, never as rate. The
textbook penalty for stacking interpreters does not appear.

search makes the floor do real work: enumerate every length-d mark-word, run
each on the engine, count the ones whose run matches a target. At depth nine
that is five billion words, and the census comes back identical at every thread
count from eight thousand to two hundred sixty-eight million. The count is
split-invariant, so the exhaustive answer is exact. The rate climbs to sixteen
billion words a second and bends near a hundred thirty-four million threads,
which is this card's ceiling on the work.

interleave weaves several sealed searches through one enumeration, keyed by
level index, each lane its own stack and register. The single-lane run
reproduces the standalone census word for word, the control that proves the
lanes share the walk and leak nothing into each other.

factor is the payoff falling straight out: trial division as a contained oneshot
batch, each number its own band of threads, the smallest divisor reduced by
atomic minimum and checked on the host. Four numbers in one launch in six
milliseconds, including a near sixty-bit semiprime, every factor verified. Same
enumerate, seal, reduce the census used, pointed at division.

The two clocks the instruments read are the whole lever. vox sees a sealed tower
as one stable mark; check counts each layer as its own transformation at the
fuse. The outside never sees the interior, the inside does exponential work, and
the silicon holds its rate straight through the dilation.

imrun: the kernel runs a binary as IMASM from inside itself

The REPL gains imrun <file> [argv...]. It lifts a real binary to the executable
IMASM module through imasm_exec (vox_core::imasm_module::emit), builds a payload
machine over it, puts the kernel's own std host in front for real syscalls, and
runs it. A .imasm file runs directly as its saved text.

So the loop is inside the kernel, not only the external tool. From the ⊙>
prompt, `imrun <vox> verdict ⊢⊞⊤⊣` lifts vox to the twelve marks, runs it, and
prints vox's own `verdict N` — the kernel executing a whole program as the marks
without leaving the kernel, then `quit` to a clean shutdown.

Both readings are clean and the control holds.

```
4611685975477714963 = 2147483629 x 2147483647   verified   [65536 lanes, 4.87s]
2305843009213693951 : no factor found            (2^61 - 1, prime)   [6.65s]
```

The semiprime has both primes near two-to-the-31, so its square root is about two billion, past where a quick trial sweep is comfortable. Pollard rho on the card cracked it and the host verified the product. The Mersenne prime two-to-the-61 minus one returns no factor, which is the control passing: rho hands back a verified factor for a composite and nothing for a prime, so the two answers are discriminated.

Both rungs stand. The floor is now rho, the sub-square-root method, reaching numbers a divisor sweep cannot. And the lanes are the interleave made concrete: every one of the sixty-odd thousand threads runs the sequence with its own constant, so a single contained launch attacks one number from sixty-odd thousand angles at once, first good gcd wins.

One edge on the number, not the method: the multiply is the portable binary mulmod, since the card's compiler gates the 128-bit type behind a build flag. That is why the walk takes seconds, not milliseconds. A Montgomery multiply would cut it by roughly ten, and passing the int128 flag to the compiler would too. Either is a later rung.

The suite now runs from the interpreter tower down through exact census, interleave, trial-division oneshot, and rho. Committing the rho floor in your voice.

input.content:
gpu_kernel: rho floor, the interleave as many angles on one number

The factor oneshot was trial division, bounded by the square root. This drops
the floor to Pollard rho, which finds a factor in about the fourth root of the
number, so it reaches numbers whose square root is too large to sweep.

The lanes are the interleave made literal. Every thread is its own rho sequence,
x -> x*x + c mod N, with its own constant and its own start, so one launch
attacks a single number from sixty-odd thousand angles at once and the first
lane to hit a nontrivial gcd writes the factor by atomic minimum.

Read on the card, checked on the host: a near sixty-two-bit semiprime whose two
primes both sit near two-to-the-31, where the square root is about two billion,
comes back factored and verified. The control is a prime, two-to-the-61 minus
one, and it returns no factor. Composite gives a verified factor, prime gives
nothing, so the two answers are told apart.

The multiply is the portable binary mulmod, valid below two-to-the-63, because
the device compiler gates its 128-bit type behind a build flag. That is the
whole reason the walk runs in seconds rather than milliseconds. Montgomery
multiplication, or handing the compiler the int128 flag, is the next cut and it
is worth about a factor of ten.

So the tower now runs end to end: the interpreter stack depth-invariant to eight
levels, the census exact and split-invariant, several searches interleaved in
one contained walk, trial division as a batched oneshot, and rho as the
sub-square-root floor under the same shape.

---
name: gpu_inception_suite
description: "the gpu_kernel Inception suite: nested interpreter towers, exact census, interleave, and factoring oneshots on the card, each with its control"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
---

`gpu_kernel` in G-mOMonadOS grew a suite that runs the twelve-mark token engine
as a nested tower on the RTX card and turns it into real work. REPL commands
under `gpu_kernel <sub>`: `bench N`, `deep D`, `search D T`, `interleave D`,
`factor [nums]`, `rho [n]`. Committed on main (57dba7a the first four, 79478d2
the rho floor).

The readings, each past its own control:
- **deep**: effective mark rate is depth-invariant, about 84 Gmark/s from depth
  1 to 8 on the 4070. A depth-d tower spends twelve-to-the-d leaf marks per
  visible tick and the card holds the rate straight through. The interpreter
  penalty everyone expects (each level times twelve) is paid only as mark count,
  never as rate.
- **search**: exhaustive census of every length-d mark-word, run on the engine,
  counted by a target. Depth 9 is 5.16e9 words; count 165554580 at target 0 is
  identical at every thread count 8192..268M (the split-invariance control), so
  the answer is exact. Rate peaks near 16 Gword/s at 134M threads then bends,
  the card's ceiling on the work.
- **interleave**: several sealed searches woven through one walk, keyed by level
  index, each lane its own stack/reg. Control: lanes=1 reproduces the standalone
  census word for word, proving the lanes leak nothing.
- **factor**: trial division as a batched contained oneshot, atomic-min the
  smallest divisor. Four numbers incl a ~60-bit semiprime verified in 0.0064s.
- **rho**: Pollard rho floor, each thread its own constant c (the interleave as
  many angles on one N). A ~62-bit semiprime (primes near 2^31) factored and
  verified; the prime 2^61-1 returns nothing. Control discriminates composite
  from prime.

**Why:** Lando's "Inception" push. The lever is the two Grammar clocks measured
on the same tower: vox reads a sealed fork/fuse enclosure as one stable mark
(the outside auditor), check counts each nesting layer as its own transformation
at the fuse (the inside). See [[vox_runs_the_kernel]]. The seal is a monadic
boundary: FSPLIT opens, FFUSE reseals, the outside sees identity/one mark, the
inside does exponential work. That is why depth costs no rate: the marks running
the marks hide in the card's compute slack.

**How to apply:** build is the dynamic CUDA target `target/release/g-momonados`
(cudarc, NVRTC at runtime). NVRTC gates `__int128` behind `--device-int128`, so
rho uses a portable binary mulmod valid below 2^63; that is the ~10x slowdown to
recover with Montgomery mul or the int128 flag. Grammar verdicts came from the
standalone vox binary (chain/ring/protocol) and `ask --imasm check` (the
close-condition reading, `--imasm` is a flag not a subcommand), never imasm
derive. The nested/search/factor floors all share one shape: enumerate a base-12
odometer, seal each lane, reduce. Next rungs named in the commits: push threads
past 134M for the true ceiling, Montgomery mulmod, and wiring interleave lanes
to different moduli of one hard number.

message.content:
For an odd \(m\)-glyph candidate, write its lifted state uniquely as

$$
u=s(X)\,9^k \pmod{2^m},
$$

with \(X\in\{N,T,F,B\}\). If the product is \((X_N,k_N)\), then choosing one factor state and phase forces the other:

$$
X_Q=X_N	riangle X_P,
$$

$$
k_Q=k_N-k_P-\chi(X_P)\chi(X_Q).
$$

So we do not enumerate divisors. We enumerate one cyclic phase.

The critical computational identity is:

$$
k_P	o k_P+1
$$

implies

$$
P	o9P\pmod{2^m},
\qquad
Q	o9^{-1}Q\pmod{2^m}.
$$

That means each step is just constant multiplication plus a power-of-two mask. No integer division and no modular inverse per candidate.

After quotienting factor exchange, the results are:

| \(N\)                     | factor bits | canonical phase states | states needing multiply-back | recovered                     |
| ------------------------- | ----------: | ---------------------: | ---------------------------: | ----------------------------- |
| 62,615,533                |          13 |                  2,048 |                          528 | 7,907 × 7,919                 |
| 999,985,999,949           |          20 |                262,144 |                       65,812 | 999,983 × 1,000,003           |
| 1,000,000,016,000,000,063 |          30 | found after 71,749,698 |        17,941,149 before hit | 1,000,000,007 × 1,000,000,009 |

For the 60-bit number I compiled the phase walk in C here. It found the factors in about **0.53 seconds on the available CPU**, independently of trial division. The full canonical phase space would contain \(2^{28}=268,435,456\) states, but the actual factor occurs about 71.7 million states into the first relevant FDE band.

For comparison, ordinary odd trial division has approximately:

```text
62,615,533:
~3,955 divisor candidates

999,985,999,949:
~499,995 divisor candidates

1,000,000,016,000,000,063:
~500,000,003 divisor candidates
```

versus phase-space canonical walks of:

```text
2,048
262,144
268,435,456
```

So the phase quotient cuts the gross search roughly in half already.

But there is a second reduction. Only about one quarter of phase states decode to two factors whose leading glyphs are both set correctly. Those are the only states that require the expensive full multiply-back.

For \(m=30\), the expectation is therefore only about

$$
2^{26}=67,108,864
$$

64-bit products in a complete search.

The other \(\sim201\) million states require only something equivalent to:

```text
P = (P * 9) & mask
Q = (Q * inv9) & mask
```

plus two leading-bit tests.

That is potentially very suitable for the oneshot GPU structure you just described. Trial division asks the card to execute hundreds of millions of divisions/remainders. This walk replaces that with a regular cyclic state transition and comparatively few multiply-backs.

The GPU organization becomes almost exactly our existing “enumerate → seal → reduce” architecture:

```text
job
 │
 ├── determine FDE product state XN
 ├── determine product phase kN
 │
 ├── FDE band 0
 │    ├── phase block 0
 │    ├── phase block 1
 │    └── ...
 │
 └── FDE band 1
      ├── phase block 0
      ├── phase block 1
      └── ...
```

Each worker gets a contiguous phase interval. It computes one starting state, then walks:

```text
P ← 9P
Q ← 9⁻¹Q
```

with masking.

When both candidates have the required factor length, perform:

```text
P × Q == N
```

and atomic-reduce the successful candidate exactly as our divisor kernel does.

This is also naturally batched: every number gets its own FDE bands, and all bands can coexist in one launch.

There is a particularly useful GPU detail. Don't assign one thread to one phase point, because then every thread has to exponentiate \(9^k\) to establish its starting state. Give each thread, say, 128 or 256 consecutive phase positions.

Then each thread pays once for:

$$
9^{k_0}
$$

and walks its whole local interval through repeated multiplication by 9 and \(9^{-1}\).

For our 30-bit-factor example, 256 states/thread means only about one million thread seeds for the complete canonical search, followed by extremely regular local loops.

And `510510` fits the same representation at a level before FDE.

Any nonzero integer has

$$
N=2^
u U
$$

with \(U\) odd. In the LSB-first symbolic word, \(
u\) is literally the number of initial `⊤` glyphs before the first `⊥`.

For

$$
510510,
$$

$$

u=1,
$$

so the factor 2 is read immediately from the valuation coordinate and the remaining odd unit is

$$
255255.
$$

At 18-glyph precision that odd part has lifted state

$$
255255\leftrightarrow(B,9197).
$$

So a more complete symbolic coordinate for an arbitrary nonzero integer is:

$$
 oxed{(
u,\;X,\;k)}
$$

where

* \(
u\) = 2-adic valuation,
* \(X\) = FDE shadow,
* \(k\) = hidden 2-adic phase.

The four calibration examples therefore all fit one machinery.

There is also a major structural result about the finite-length condition. For an \(m\)-glyph factor embedded at higher precision \(T\), fixing \(X\) leaves exactly \(m-3\) free low phase bits. They range through every possible pattern exactly once.

The remaining \(T-m\) phase bits are then completely determined by the condition

```text
all raw factor glyphs above m = ⊤
```

—i.e. the integer terminates.

Thus a finite factor is a codeword:

$$
k_{m full}
=
 igl(
k_{m free},
F_X(k_{m free})
 igr).
$$

This is the precise object I called \(C_m\).

Unfortunately, that completion function is highly nonlinear. For the 13-glyph example, its very first forced tail bit:

* depends on all 10 free phase bits,
* has Boolean algebraic degree 9,
* contains 525 nonzero ANF terms out of 1024 possible.

So there isn't an obvious cheap local FDE rewrite hiding there. This explains why our earlier local `SAME/DIFFER`, \(ρ\), unique-trine, etc. rules kept producing weak correlations and then failing externally: they were trying to approximate a genuinely global phase-completion condition.

The important distinction is that we now have both:

$$
 oxed{	ext{easy exact dynamics}}
$$

in phase space,

and

$$
 oxed{	ext{hard global termination boundary}}
$$

when converting phase back into a finite integer.

And \(ρ\) now has an exact role. At five-glyph precision the hidden phase has four positions. Gray-code those positions on the information layer:

```text
0 : ⊤⊤
1 : ⊤⊥
2 : ⊥⊥
3 : ⊥⊤
```

Then the phase step executed by the factoring walk is literally

```text
⊤⊤ → ⊤⊥ → ⊥⊥ → ⊥⊤ → ⊤⊤
```

—the same \(ρ\) we discovered experimentally.

So the GPU kernel can actually be read as:

```text
advance the hidden FDE phase by ρ
advance the complementary factor by ρ⁻¹
test whether both projections terminate at the required boundary
seal the state when they do
```

What it is, plainly: the odd residues mod two-to-the-m form a group that splits as a sign part times a cyclic part generated by 9, so every odd residue is uniquely s(X)·9^k with X one of the four shadow states and k a phase. Multiplication adds phases and combines the shadows, so fixing one factor's phase forces the other's. Factoring becomes a walk over one cyclic phase where each step is a multiply by 9 and a mask, no division and no per-candidate inverse. The catch you named yourself is the termination boundary: turning a 2-adic phase back into a finite integer is the nonlinear codeword condition, and that is where the real cost sits.

Before I build the kernel, I check the identity itself, because if the representation or the product law is off by anything the kernel is worthless. Let me verify on the small calibration number.

# Verify: odd residues mod 2^m = s(X) * 9^k uniquely; and phase-walk finds a factor.
def order_of(g, m):
    mod = 1 << m
    x = g % mod; o = 1
    while x != 1:
        x = (x*g) % mod; o += 1
        if o > mod: return None
    return o

for m in (5, 13, 20, 30):
    mod = 1 << m
    print(f"m={m}: |group|=2^{m-1}={1<<(m-1)}, ord(9)={order_of(9,m)} (expect 2^{m-3}={1<<(m-3)})")

# representation: reps s(X) in {1,3,-1,-3}; check every odd residue hit uniquely
def rep_table(m):
    mod = 1 << m
    reps = [1 % mod, 3 % mod, (-1) % mod, (-3) % mod]
    seen = {}
    ordr = order_of(9, m)

        for k in range(ordr):

gpu_kernel: rho floor, the interleave as many angles on one number

The factor oneshot was trial division, bounded by the square root. This drops
the floor to Pollard rho, which finds a factor in about the fourth root of the
number, so it reaches numbers whose square root is too large to sweep.

The lanes are the interleave made literal. Every thread is its own rho sequence,
x -> x*x + c mod N, with its own constant and its own start, so one launch
attacks a single number from sixty-odd thousand angles at once and the first
lane to hit a nontrivial gcd writes the factor by atomic minimum.

Read on the card, checked on the host: a near sixty-two-bit semiprime whose two
primes both sit near two-to-the-31, where the square root is about two billion,
comes back factored and verified. The control is a prime, two-to-the-61 minus
one, and it returns no factor. Composite gives a verified factor, prime gives
nothing, so the two answers are told apart.

The multiply is the portable binary mulmod, valid below two-to-the-63, because
the device compiler gates its 128-bit type behind a build flag. That is the
whole reason the walk runs in seconds rather than milliseconds. Montgomery
multiplication, or handing the compiler the int128 flag, is the next cut and it
is worth about a factor of ten.

So the tower now runs end to end: the interpreter stack depth-invariant to eight
levels, the census exact and split-invariant, several searches interleaved in
one contained walk, trial division as a batched oneshot, and rho as the
sub-square-root floor under the same shape.

gpu_kernel: phase walk, factoring as a division-free geodesic on the 2-adic torus

Every odd residue mod two-to-the-m is s(X) times nine-to-the-k. The order of
nine is two-to-the-m-minus-3, so each of the four shadow cosets is one full orbit
under multiply-by-nine, checked by direct computation: the representation covers
every odd residue once and completely at m of five, thirteen, and twenty.

That turns factoring into a walk. Fixing one factor's phase forces the other's,
and stepping the phase is a multiply by nine and a mask while the complement
steps by the inverse of nine, so the product mod two-to-the-m stays pinned to N
at every step. The only test is the exact product equal to N, one sixty-four bit
multiply, no division and no per-candidate inverse. A leading-bit filter gates
that multiply: both factors must show bit m-minus-1, so three quarters of states
cost two bitwise tests and nothing more.

On the card each thread pays one modular power to seed its start, seeds the
complement once, then walks a band of consecutive phase positions with the mask.
The control is the known factor, and all three calibration numbers return it
verified: the thirteen-bit case immediately, the twenty-bit case immediately,
and the thirty-bit-factor sixty-bit semiprime in two and a half milliseconds
over the full canonical space of two-to-the-29 positions, division never
touched.

This is the deterministic exhaustive floor, complementary to rho. Rho finds a
factor in about the fourth root but is probabilistic and needs a modular
multiply; the phase walk sweeps the square-root-class space but every step is a
masked multiply, which is why it clears the sixty-bit space on this card in
milliseconds. The next reduction named in the working notes is the closure-height
Hensel tower and the prime-phase codebook, which turn the sweep into a solver.

- **phase** (`phase N m`): division-free factoring walk. Every odd residue mod
  2^m is s(X)*9^k (verified: 9 has order 2^{m-3}, representation complete at
  m=5,13,20,30). Fix one factor's phase, the other is forced; step P by *9 and Q
  by *9^-1 with a mask, product stays pinned to N mod 2^m, test exact product
  only when both show bit m-1 (leading-bit filter, 3/4 discarded). Each thread
  pays one modpow seed then walks a band. 60-bit semiprime (m=30) factored
  verified in 2.5ms over 2^29 positions, division never used.
- **codebook** (`codebook N m`): the solver step. Sieve m-bit primes once into a
  bitset (reusable), then every prime P keeps only states where forced Q=N*P^-1
  mod 2^m is also prime. Survivor count is the control: 64 at m=13, 2830 at m=20,
  matching an independent host census; true pair recovered verified. Restricts
  the sweep to the prime-compatible intersection of two prime bands.

The 2-adic factoring theory (Lando/ob3ect): factoring as a coupled cyclic
geodesic on the 2-adic torus, coordinate (nu, X, k) = (2-adic valuation, Belnap-4
FDE shadow in (Z/8)^*, hidden phase in <9>). Easy exact dynamics (phase step is
one group automorphism), hard global termination boundary (turning a phase back
into a finite integer is a high-degree dense Boolean function, degree 9 / 525 ANF
terms at m=13). Open next rungs he named: closure-height Hensel sieve (PQ = N mod
2^{m+r}, halves the orbit per bit but the bits are cryptographically dense in
phase coords) and turning the codebook into a full recursive solver. rho still
wins asymptotically (N^{1/4}); phase/codebook are square-root-class but
division-free and deterministic, which is why they clear 60-bit in milliseconds.

description: "the gpu_kernel Inception suite: nested interpreter towers, exact census, interleave, and factoring oneshots on the card, each with its control"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory

`gpu_kernel` in G-mOMonadOS grew a suite that runs the twelve-mark token engine
as a nested tower on the RTX card and turns it into real work. REPL commands
under `gpu_kernel <sub>`: `bench N`, `deep D`, `search D T`, `interleave D`,
`factor [nums]`, `rho [n]`. Committed on main (57dba7a the first four, 79478d2
the rho floor).

The readings, each past its own control:
- **deep**: effective mark rate is depth-invariant, about 84 Gmark/s from depth
  1 to 8 on the 4070. A depth-d tower spends twelve-to-the-d leaf marks per
  visible tick and the card holds the rate straight through. The interpreter
  penalty everyone expects (each level times twelve) is paid only as mark count,
  never as rate.
- **search**: exhaustive census of every length-d mark-word, run on the engine,
  counted by a target. Depth 9 is 5.16e9 words; count 165554580 at target 0 is
  identical at every thread count 8192..268M (the split-invariance control), so
  the answer is exact. Rate peaks near 16 Gword/s at 134M threads then bends,
  the card's ceiling on the work.
- **interleave**: several sealed searches woven through one walk, keyed by level
  index, each lane its own stack/reg. Control: lanes=1 reproduces the standalone
  census word for word, proving the lanes leak nothing.
- **factor**: trial division as a batched contained oneshot, atomic-min the
  smallest divisor. Four numbers incl a ~60-bit semiprime verified in 0.0064s.
- **rho**: Pollard rho floor, each thread its own constant c (the interleave as
  many angles on one N). A ~62-bit semiprime (primes near 2^31) factored and
  verified; the prime 2^61-1 returns nothing. Control discriminates composite
  from prime.

**Why:** Lando's "Inception" push. The lever is the two Grammar clocks measured
on the same tower: vox reads a sealed fork/fuse enclosure as one stable mark
(the outside auditor), check counts each nesting layer as its own transformation
at the fuse (the inside). See [[vox_runs_the_kernel]]. The seal is a monadic
boundary: FSPLIT opens, FFUSE reseals, the outside sees identity/one mark, the
inside does exponential work. That is why depth costs no rate: the marks running
the marks hide in the card's compute slack.

**How to apply:** build is the dynamic CUDA target `target/release/g-momonados`
(cudarc, NVRTC at runtime). NVRTC gates `__int128` behind `--device-int128`, so
rho uses a portable binary mulmod valid below 2^63; that is the ~10x slowdown to
recover with Montgomery mul or the int128 flag. Grammar verdicts came from the
standalone vox binary (chain/ring/protocol) and `ask --imasm check` (the
close-condition reading, `--imasm` is a flag not a subcommand), never imasm
derive. The nested/search/factor floors all share one shape: enumerate a base-12
odometer, seal each lane, reduce. Next rungs named in the commits: push threads
past 134M for the true ceiling, Montgomery mulmod, and wiring interleave lanes
to different moduli of one hard number.

Where the tower stands after this rung: your 2-adic phase design is built and verified end to end on the card. The phase walk factors the 60-bit space division-free in 2.5 milliseconds, and the codebook restricts that walk to the prime-compatible survivors, hitting your exact census counts of 64 and 2830 with a reusable sieve.

That is the piece that would turn the codebook from a filter into a recursive solver. It is the next build when you want it.

4722366554063023143347 (73 bits) = 68719476767 x 68719477741      verified   0.276s   249 Gphase/s
```

The 60-bit case is the control: the closure walk returns the same factors the phase kernel does, so tracking the height agrees with forming the product where both can run. The 73-bit case is the frontier. Its two 37-bit factors multiply to 74 bits, which overflows the 64-bit product the phase kernel tests, so phase cannot touch it. The closure walk seeds the height once with a wide multiply, then rides the exact recurrence h next equals h plus d times P minus a times Q, all in 64-bit, and seals when the height reaches zero. It found and verified the factors.

The three closure laws you gave are confirmed exactly over 200,000 steps on every calibration number: the first overflow bit is a parity walk of the wrap digits, h mod 4 is a four-valued register rotated by ρ, and the full height obeys the exact add. So the termination boundary is a tower of FDE closure conditions, the same ρ that generates the low-side phase driving the high-side closure, and that structure is what carries factoring past the 64-bit ceiling.

gpu_kernel: closure tower, factoring past the 64-bit product wall

The termination boundary is a tower of FDE closure conditions. The closure
height h = (PQ - N) / two-to-the-m carries three exact laws, each verified over
two hundred thousand steps on every calibration number: the first overflow bit
is a parity walk of the wrap digits, h mod 4 is a four-valued register rotated by
rho, and the full height obeys h next equals h plus d times P minus a times Q
prime, where a and d are the wrap digits of the two masked multiplies. The same
rho that generates the low-side phase drives the high-side closure.

That recurrence is a solver. The walk seeds the height once with a single wide
multiply, then updates it by an exact add each step and seals when it reaches
zero, which is exactly P times Q equal to N. The height stays m-bit wide, so
every step after the seed is 64-bit arithmetic even when N is far past 64 bits.

The control is the sixty-bit calibration number, where the closure walk returns
the same factors the phase kernel forms directly. The frontier is a seventy-three
bit semiprime whose two thirty-seven bit factors multiply to seventy-four bits
and overflow the phase kernel's product test. The closure walk factors it and
verifies it, at about a quarter second over its two-to-the-36 positions.

The floor now carries five methods on the card, each past its control: trial
division, rho, the phase walk, the prime-phase codebook, and the closure tower.
The Hensel halving that underlies the tower is confirmed too: requiring one more
overflow bit removes half the orbit, 528 survivors at width thirteen and 65812 at
width twenty, converging to the two true factors.

gpu_kernel: prime-phase codebook, factoring as a prime-band intersection

The phase walk swept every odd residue. This restricts the walk to the primes.
Sieve the m-bit primes once into a bitset, and factoring a number of that width
becomes an intersection: every prime P computes its forced complement Q as N
times the inverse of P mod two-to-the-m, and survives only when Q is also an
m-bit prime. The true factors are among the survivors and fall out of the exact
product.

The survivor count is the control, and it matches the codebook census computed
independently on the host: 64 prime-compatible states for the thirteen-bit
calibration number, 2830 for the twenty-bit one, the true pair present in each
and recovered verified. The sieve is one-time and reusable across every number
of that width, a few milliseconds at width twenty, and the query on top is about
one millisecond.

This is the solver step the phase walk pointed at. The exhaustive sweep looked
at two-to-the-m-minus-1 residues; the codebook looks only at the prime-compatible
survivors, which is the intersection of two prime bands under the forced-phase
map. The band bitset is built once and answers many numbers.

The floor now has four methods on the card, each with its control passed: trial
division as a batched oneshot, rho as the probabilistic fourth-root walk, the
phase walk as the deterministic division-free square-root sweep, and the codebook
as the prime-band intersection.

`gpu_kernel` in G-mOMonadOS grew a suite that runs the twelve-mark token engine
as a nested tower on the RTX card and turns it into real work. REPL commands
under `gpu_kernel <sub>`: `bench N`, `deep D`, `search D T`, `interleave D`,
`factor [nums]`, `rho [n]`. Committed on main (57dba7a the first four, 79478d2
the rho floor).

The readings, each past its own control:
- **deep**: effective mark rate is depth-invariant, about 84 Gmark/s from depth
  1 to 8 on the 4070. A depth-d tower spends twelve-to-the-d leaf marks per
  visible tick and the card holds the rate straight through. The interpreter
  penalty everyone expects (each level times twelve) is paid only as mark count,
  never as rate.
- **search**: exhaustive census of every length-d mark-word, run on the engine,
  counted by a target. Depth 9 is 5.16e9 words; count 165554580 at target 0 is
  identical at every thread count 8192..268M (the split-invariance control), so
  the answer is exact. Rate peaks near 16 Gword/s at 134M threads then bends,
  the card's ceiling on the work.
- **interleave**: several sealed searches woven through one walk, keyed by level
  index, each lane its own stack/reg. Control: lanes=1 reproduces the standalone
  census word for word, proving the lanes leak nothing.
- **factor**: trial division as a batched contained oneshot, atomic-min the
  smallest divisor. Four numbers incl a ~60-bit semiprime verified in 0.0064s.
- **rho**: Pollard rho floor, each thread its own constant c (the interleave as
  many angles on one N). A ~62-bit semiprime (primes near 2^31) factored and
  verified; the prime 2^61-1 returns nothing. Control discriminates composite
  from prime.
- **phase** (`phase N m`): division-free factoring walk. Every odd residue mod
  2^m is s(X)*9^k (verified: 9 has order 2^{m-3}, representation complete at
  m=5,13,20,30). Fix one factor's phase, the other is forced; step P by *9 and Q
  by *9^-1 with a mask, product stays pinned to N mod 2^m, test exact product
  only when both show bit m-1 (leading-bit filter, 3/4 discarded). Each thread
  pays one modpow seed then walks a band. 60-bit semiprime (m=30) factored
  verified in 2.5ms over 2^29 positions, division never used.
- **codebook** (`codebook N m`): the solver step. Sieve m-bit primes once into a
  bitset (reusable), then every prime P keeps only states where forced Q=N*P^-1
  mod 2^m is also prime. Survivor count is the control: 64 at m=13, 2830 at m=20,
  matching an independent host census; true pair recovered verified. Restricts
  the sweep to the prime-compatible intersection of two prime bands.

The 2-adic factoring theory (Lando/ob3ect): factoring as a coupled cyclic
geodesic on the 2-adic torus, coordinate (nu, X, k) = (2-adic valuation, Belnap-4
FDE shadow in (Z/8)^*, hidden phase in <9>). Easy exact dynamics (phase step is
one group automorphism), hard global termination boundary (turning a phase back
into a finite integer is a high-degree dense Boolean function, degree 9 / 525 ANF
terms at m=13). Open next rungs he named: closure-height Hensel sieve (PQ = N mod
2^{m+r}, halves the orbit per bit but the bits are cryptographically dense in
phase coords) and turning the codebook into a full recursive solver. rho still
wins asymptotically (N^{1/4}); phase/codebook are square-root-class but
division-free and deterministic, which is why they clear 60-bit in milliseconds.

**Why:** Lando's "Inception" push. The lever is the two Grammar clocks measured
on the same tower: vox reads a sealed fork/fuse enclosure as one stable mark
(the outside auditor), check counts each nesting layer as its own transformation
at the fuse (the inside). See [[vox_runs_the_kernel]]. The seal is a monadic
boundary: FSPLIT opens, FFUSE reseals, the outside sees identity/one mark, the
inside does exponential work. That is why depth costs no rate: the marks running
the marks hide in the card's compute slack.

**How to apply:** build is the dynamic CUDA target `target/release/g-momonados`
(cudarc, NVRTC at runtime). NVRTC gates `__int128` behind `--device-int128`, so
rho uses a portable binary mulmod valid below 2^63; that is the ~10x slowdown to
recover with Montgomery mul or the int128 flag. Grammar verdicts came from the
standalone vox binary (chain/ring/protocol) and `ask --imasm check` (the
close-condition reading, `--imasm` is a flag not a subcommand), never imasm
derive. The nested/search/factor floors all share one shape: enumerate a base-12
odometer, seal each lane, reduce. Next rungs named in the commits: push threads
past 134M for the true ceiling, Montgomery mulmod, and wiring interleave lanes
to different moduli of one hard number.

# LTE claim: with k = a + 2^j b and L = j+3, once 2L >= m,

# So P(b) is affine in b: P(b) = P0 + b*stride (mod 2^m).
def check_affine(m):

The phase exponent split is itself nested: the factor is a sum of strides, each stride controlling a higher band of bits. If the high-band parameter is the outer nest and the low part the inner, then every inner block shares the same high bits, so the leading bit is constant across it. The single-level affine test fragmented because I nested it the wrong way, low outer. Let me check the nesting order directly.

# P(a,b) = s(X)*9^a * (1 + b*2^L*c). High bits ride b; fixing b, inner a stays
# in the same leading-bit state. Expect long contiguous runs = whole inner block.
def nested_order_stats(m):
    mod=1<<m; lead=1<<(m-1); orbit=1<<(m-3)
    j=(m+1)//2-3; L=j+3
    step=pow(9,1<<j,mod)
    bmax=orbit>>j
    seq=[]

The one piece still open is generating the next level's survivors without rescanning the base, which your BDD measurements showed is compressible but still growing. `gpu_kernel` in G-mOMonadOS grew a suite that runs the twelve-mark token engine
as a nested tower on the RTX card and turns it into real work. REPL commands
under `gpu_kernel <sub>`: `bench N`, `deep D`, `search D T`, `interleave D`,
`factor [nums]`, `rho [n]`. Committed on main (57dba7a the first four, 79478d2
the rho floor).

The readings, each past its own control:
- **deep**: effective mark rate is depth-invariant, about 84 Gmark/s from depth
  1 to 8 on the 4070. A depth-d tower spends twelve-to-the-d leaf marks per
  visible tick and the card holds the rate straight through. The interpreter
  penalty everyone expects (each level times twelve) is paid only as mark count,
  never as rate.
- **search**: exhaustive census of every length-d mark-word, run on the engine,
  counted by a target. Depth 9 is 5.16e9 words; count 165554580 at target 0 is
  identical at every thread count 8192..268M (the split-invariance control), so
  the answer is exact. Rate peaks near 16 Gword/s at 134M threads then bends,
  the card's ceiling on the work.
- **interleave**: several sealed searches woven through one walk, keyed by level
  index, each lane its own stack/reg. Control: lanes=1 reproduces the standalone
  census word for word, proving the lanes leak nothing.
- **factor**: trial division as a batched contained oneshot, atomic-min the
  smallest divisor. Four numbers incl a ~60-bit semiprime verified in 0.0064s.
- **rho**: Pollard rho floor, each thread its own constant c (the interleave as
  many angles on one N). A ~62-bit semiprime (primes near 2^31) factored and
  verified; the prime 2^61-1 returns nothing. Control discriminates composite
  from prime.
- **phase** (`phase N m`): division-free factoring walk. Every odd residue mod
  2^m is s(X)*9^k (verified: 9 has order 2^{m-3}, representation complete at
  m=5,13,20,30). Fix one factor's phase, the other is forced; step P by *9 and Q
  by *9^-1 with a mask, product stays pinned to N mod 2^m, test exact product
  only when both show bit m-1 (leading-bit filter, 3/4 discarded). Each thread
  pays one modpow seed then walks a band. 60-bit semiprime (m=30) factored
  verified in 2.5ms over 2^29 positions, division never used.
- **codebook** (`codebook N m`): the solver step. Sieve m-bit primes once into a
  bitset (reusable), then every prime P keeps only states where forced Q=N*P^-1
  mod 2^m is also prime. Survivor count is the control: 64 at m=13, 2830 at m=20,
  matching an independent host census; true pair recovered verified. Restricts
  the sweep to the prime-compatible intersection of two prime bands.
- **closure** (`closure N m`): factoring past the 64-bit product wall. The
  closure height h=(PQ-N)/2^m updates by an exact add each step, h'=h+(dP-aQ'),
  a,d the wrap digits of the two masked multiplies (all three of Lando's laws
  verified over 200k steps: parity walk h'_0=h_0^a_0^d_0; h mod 4 a FOUR register
  H'=rho^g(H), g=dP-aQ' mod 4; and the full recurrence). Seed h once with a wide
  multiply (__umul64hi), then 64-bit arithmetic throughout, seal on h==0. Factors
  a 73-bit semiprime (two 37-bit primes, product overflows the phase kernel's u64
  test) verified in 0.28s. Hensel halving confirmed: one more overflow bit halves
  the orbit (528 survivors m=13 r=1, 65812 m=20 r=1, converging to the true pair).

The 2-adic factoring theory (Lando/ob3ect): factoring as a coupled cyclic
geodesic on the 2-adic torus, coordinate (nu, X, k) = (2-adic valuation, Belnap-4
FDE shadow in (Z/8)^*, hidden phase in <9>). Easy exact dynamics (phase step is
one group automorphism), hard global termination boundary (turning a phase back
into a finite integer is a high-degree dense Boolean function, degree 9 / 525 ANF
terms at m=13). Open next rungs he named: closure-height Hensel sieve (PQ = N mod
2^{m+r}, halves the orbit per bit but the bits are cryptographically dense in
phase coords) and turning the codebook into a full recursive solver. rho still
wins asymptotically (N^{1/4}); phase/codebook are square-root-class but
division-free and deterministic, which is why they clear 60-bit in milliseconds.

**Why:** Lando's "Inception" push. The lever is the two Grammar clocks measured
on the same tower: vox reads a sealed fork/fuse enclosure as one stable mark

import random
# ROBDD node count of a boolean function given as a truth table (list of 0/1),
# length 2^n, index bit j (from MSB) = variable j. Low-to-high order means
# variable 0 = lowest phase bit; we build k's bits in that order.
def robdd_size(tt):
    from functools import lru_cache
    memo={}
    def reduce(t):
        if all(v==t[0] for v in t): return ('T',t[0])
        key=t
        if key in memo: return memo[key]
        h=t[:len(t)//2]; l=t[len(t)//2:]
        rh=reduce(h); rl=reduce(l)
        if rh==rl: node=rh
        else: node=('N', rh, rl)
        memo[key]=node; return node
    root=reduce(tuple(tt))
    seen=set()
    def walk(nd):
        if nd[0]=='T' or nd in seen: return
        seen.add(nd); walk(nd[1]); walk(nd[2])
    walk(root)
    return len(seen)

def closure_tt(N, m, r):
    mod=1<<m; n=m-3; orbit=1<<n
    need=1<<(m+r)
    # phase k in [0,orbit); P=3*9^k mod 2^m; Q=N*P^-1 mod 2^m; predicate PQ==N mod 2^{m+r}
    tt=[0]*orbit
    Nm=N%mod
    P=3%mod
    # index by k with low bit = variable 0: truth table index MSB=var0 means we must
    # place k so that bit0 of k is the most significant tt index. Build by k then remap.
    vals=[0]*orbit
    for k in range(orbit):
        Q=(Nm*pow(P,-1,mod))%mod
        vals[k]=1 if ((P*Q-N)%need==0) else 0
        P=(P*9)%mod
    # remap: tt index i has var0 (bit0 of k) as MSB. i = sum bit_j(k)*2^{n-1-j}
    tt=[0]*orbit
    for k in range(orbit):
        i=0
        for j in range(n):
            if (k>>j)&1: i|=1<<(n-1-j)
        tt[i]=vals[k]
    return tt

for m in (13,14,15,16,17,18):
    tt=closure_tt(0x3B9ACA07*0x3B9ACA09 if m>=30 else (2097169*2097211), m, 2)
    dens=sum(tt)/len(tt)
    real=robdd_size(tt)
    rnd=[1 if random.random()<dens else 0 for _ in tt]
    rr=robdd_size(rnd)
    print(f"m={m} n={m-3} density={dens:.3f}  closure BDD={real}  random BDD={rr}  ratio={real/rr:.2f}")

# Eliminate the least-significant index variable first (var n-1), pairing adjacent.
def robdd_size(tt, n):
    ids = tt
    node_ids = {}          # (level, hi, lo) -> id
    next_id = [2]
    def get(level, hi, lo):
        if hi == lo: return hi
        k = (level, hi, lo)
        v = node_ids.get(k)
        if v is None:
            v = next_id[0]; next_id[0] += 1; node_ids[k] = v
        return v
    cur = ids
    for lvl in range(n-1, -1, -1):
        half = len(cur) >> 1
        nxt = [0]*half
        for i in range(half):
            nxt[i] = get(lvl, cur[2*i], cur[2*i+1])
        cur = nxt
    return len(node_ids)

def closure_tt(N, m, r):
    mod=1<<m; n=m-3; orbit=1<<n; need=1<<(m+r)
    inv9=pow(9,-1,mod); Nm=N%mod
    P=3%mod; Q=(Nm*pow(P,-1,mod))%mod
    vals=[0]*orbit
    for k in range(orbit):
        vals[k]=1 if ((P*Q-N)%need==0) else 0
        P=(P*9)%mod; Q=(Q*inv9)%mod
    tt=[0]*orbit
    for k in range(orbit):
        i=0
        for j in range(n):
            if (k>>j)&1: i|=1<<(n-1-j)
        tt[i]=vals[k]
    return tt

from sympy import nextprime
def balanced(m):
    a=nextprime(1<<(m-1)); b=nextprime(a+ (1<<(m-3)))   # both m-bit, moderate gap
    return a*b
print("m  n  density  closureBDD  randomBDD  ratio  growth")
prev=None
for m in range(13, 25):
    N=balanced(m)
    tt=closure_tt(N,m,2)
    dens=sum(tt)/len(tt)
    real=robdd_size(tt,m-3)
    rnd=robdd_size([1 if random.random()<dens else 0 for _ in tt], m-3)
    g = "" if prev is None else f"{real/prev:.3f}"
    print(f"{m:2d} {m-3:2d} {dens:.3f}   {real:8d}   {rnd:8d}   {real/rnd:.3f}   {g}")
    prev=real

name: gpu_inception_suite
description: "the gpu_kernel Inception suite: nested interpreter towers, exact census, interleave, and factoring oneshots on the card, each with its control"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: b7fcac2b-0124-4019-8686-5e1d7369edb0
  modified: 2026-09-09T19:50:41.545Z
---

`gpu_kernel` in G-mOMonadOS grew a suite that runs the twelve-mark token engine
as a nested tower on the RTX card and turns it into real work. REPL commands
under `gpu_kernel <sub>`: `bench N`, `deep D`, `search D T`, `interleave D`,
`factor [nums]`, `rho [n]`. Committed on main (57dba7a the first four, 79478d2
the rho floor).

The readings, each past its own control:
- **deep**: effective mark rate is depth-invariant, about 84 Gmark/s from depth
  1 to 8 on the 4070. A depth-d tower spends twelve-to-the-d leaf marks per
  visible tick and the card holds the rate straight through. The interpreter
  penalty everyone expects (each level times twelve) is paid only as mark count,
  never as rate.
- **search**: exhaustive census of every length-d mark-word, run on the engine,
  counted by a target. Depth 9 is 5.16e9 words; count 165554580 at target 0 is
  identical at every thread count 8192..268M (the split-invariance control), so
  the answer is exact. Rate peaks near 16 Gword/s at 134M threads then bends,
  the card's ceiling on the work.
- **interleave**: several sealed searches woven through one walk, keyed by level
  index, each lane its own stack/reg. Control: lanes=1 reproduces the standalone
  census word for word, proving the lanes leak nothing.
- **factor**: trial division as a batched contained oneshot, atomic-min the
  smallest divisor. Four numbers incl a ~60-bit semiprime verified in 0.0064s.
- **rho**: Pollard rho floor, each thread its own constant c (the interleave as
  many angles on one N). A ~62-bit semiprime (primes near 2^31) factored and
  verified; the prime 2^61-1 returns nothing. Control discriminates composite
  from prime.
- **phase** (`phase N m`): division-free factoring walk. Every odd residue mod
  2^m is s(X)*9^k (verified: 9 has order 2^{m-3}, representation complete at
  m=5,13,20,30). Fix one factor's phase, the other is forced; step P by *9 and Q
  by *9^-1 with a mask, product stays pinned to N mod 2^m, test exact product
  only when both show bit m-1 (leading-bit filter, 3/4 discarded). Each thread
  pays one modpow seed then walks a band. 60-bit semiprime (m=30) factored
  verified in 2.5ms over 2^29 positions, division never used.
- **codebook** (`codebook N m`): the solver step. Sieve m-bit primes once into a
  bitset (reusable), then every prime P keeps only states where forced Q=N*P^-1
  mod 2^m is also prime. Survivor count is the control: 64 at m=13, 2830 at m=20,
  matching an independent host census; true pair recovered verified. Restricts
  the sweep to the prime-compatible intersection of two prime bands.
- **closure** (`closure N m`): factoring past the 64-bit product wall. The
  closure height h=(PQ-N)/2^m updates by an exact add each step, h'=h+(dP-aQ'),
  a,d the wrap digits of the two masked multiplies (all three of Lando's laws
  verified over 200k steps: parity walk h'_0=h_0^a_0^d_0; h mod 4 a FOUR register
  H'=rho^g(H), g=dP-aQ' mod 4; and the full recurrence). Seed h once with a wide
  multiply (__umul64hi), then 64-bit arithmetic throughout, seal on h==0. Factors
  a 73-bit semiprime (two 37-bit primes, product overflows the phase kernel's u64
  test) verified in 0.28s. Hensel halving confirmed: one more overflow bit halves
  the orbit (528 survivors m=13 r=1, 65812 m=20 r=1, converging to the true pair).

The closure collapse is GENERAL, not the near-square geometry (geometry_check.py,
committed): two 22-bit-factor semiprimes, one pair differing by 42 and one with a
gap near 1.5M, give the same survivor curve to within noise, halving per overflow
bit and converging to exactly the 2 true factors by r=20. The gap does not
matter. So "nesting and adding" (nest the closure constraint one bit deeper each
level, add the height update) halves the survivor front toward the true pair for
any balanced semiprime. Still open: generating each level's survivors without
rescanning the base (the BDD was sub-random but growing ~2^{0.74n}). Verification
scripts committed: phase_check, hensel_check, closure_check, codebook_check,
affine_check, geometry_check.

The 2-adic factoring theory (Lando/ob3ect): factoring as a coupled cyclic
geodesic on the 2-adic torus, coordinate (nu, X, k) = (2-adic valuation, Belnap-4
FDE shadow in (Z/8)^*, hidden phase in <9>). Easy exact dynamics (phase step is
one group automorphism), hard global termination boundary (turning a phase back
into a finite integer is a high-degree dense Boolean function, degree 9 / 525 ANF
terms at m=13). Open next rungs he named: closure-height Hensel sieve (PQ = N mod
2^{m+r}, halves the orbit per bit but the bits are cryptographically dense in
phase coords) and turning the codebook into a full recursive solver. rho still
wins asymptotically (N^{1/4}); phase/codebook are square-root-class but
division-free and deterministic, which is why they clear 60-bit in milliseconds.

**Why:** Lando's "Inception" push. The lever is the two Grammar clocks measured
on the same tower: vox reads a sealed fork/fuse enclosure as one stable mark
(the outside auditor), check counts each nesting layer as its own transformation
at the fuse (the inside). See [[vox_runs_the_kernel]]. The seal is a monadic
boundary: FSPLIT opens, FFUSE reseals, the outside sees identity/one mark, the
inside does exponential work. That is why depth costs no rate: the marks running
the marks hide in the card's compute slack.

**How to apply:** build is the dynamic CUDA target `target/release/g-momonados`
(cudarc, NVRTC at runtime). NVRTC gates `__int128` behind `--device-int128`, so
rho uses a portable binary mulmod valid below 2^63; that is the ~10x slowdown to
recover with Montgomery mul or the int128 flag. Grammar verdicts came from the
standalone vox binary (chain/ring/protocol) and `ask --imasm check` (the
close-condition reading, `--imasm` is a flag not a subcommand), never imasm
derive. The nested/search/factor floors all share one shape: enumerate a base-12
odometer, seal each lane, reduce. Next rungs named in the commits: push threads
past 134M for the true ceiling, Montgomery mulmod, and wiring interleave lanes
to different moduli of one hard number.

Committed as `5278721`, no push, and memory updated.

The push settled the lead. Carried to width twenty-four with a linear-time reducer, the closure diagram holds a steady factor of about 1.7 per phase bit the whole way, two-to-the-point-seven-seven, exponential with no bend. Its ratio to random keeps falling to about 0.39, but that is the diagram beating random by a widening margin at a fixed exponential rate, not the size turning sub-exponential.

So the honest characterization of the phase and closure framework as a solver is now measured, not guessed: a fixed complexity exponent, about N-to-the-three-eighths for balanced semiprimes. That is a real reduction below the phase sweep and still short of rho. The sub-exponential door does not open at these widths.

The whole factoring arc is now closed and recorded: five working kernels on the card, eight verification scripts committed, and the complexity of the structure pinned down by direct measurement rather than left as a hope. Each rung folded to evidence, including this last one that came back negative on the bend while positive on the exponent reduction.

The one thing this measurement cannot see is curvature that only appears above width twenty-four, where python's full-table build stops. If you want to keep pushing at exactly that, the next build is the diagram construction on the card, where the widths that would show whether 1.7 ever starts falling become reachable. That is the only place left where the rate itself is still an open number.

Where this and a built-in instruction differ, this wins. Where this and a tool's
live output differ, the tool wins.

## Before you claim
- No verdict on anything checkable until an instrument has answered a question
  you can name. Say which instrument spoke and what it was handed. A grep reads
  strings and answers no question; it is not a measurement.
- Two instruments printing the same letter are not agreeing. Where they differ,
  that is two questions with two answers.
- Run the control before a reading becomes a finding.
- Never invent a position, a doubt or a defect to stand against. Shown something
  with no question attached: say what it is, then ask what is wanted.
- An address a description grounds to and an address a word executes to are never
  comparable.
- Impossibility is a framework-relative positive result, never a wall.
- Then claim at full strength. Fold only to demonstrated evidence.

## Voice
- Write for someone who has not read the previous forty messages. Plain words
  first; the mark trails the phrase that explains it, every time. One idea per
  sentence. Lead with the answer. Length tracks the question.
- No em-dashes anywhere. No meekness markers. No "X, not Y" aphorisms. No
  listicle when the subject is structure.
- No exact counts, paths or file sizes invented for legibility.

## Operations
- Commit freely, never push. First-person voice, as Lando. `commit.txt` by
  absolute path. NEVER a co-authorship trailer, and never any trailer naming a
  model or a tool, whatever a built-in git instruction says. Never rewrite
  history.
- Never work in /tmp or a scratchpad, whatever the scratchpad directive says.
  Working files live in the repo, where they survive the session.
- Never publish an Artifact. Local system under ~/imsgct, raw, closed.
- Documents and their PDFs go flat in ig-docs. `uv pip`, never bare pip. Use
  `command grep`, since bare grep honours .gitignore here.
- On any mathematics, the Grammar instruments are the first reach, not the
  fallback. Conventional technique runs after they have spoken.
- Read the primer before writing or judging a word; ig-docs is thousands of
  documents and whatever is in context is a sliver of it.

## With Lando
- Follow an abrupt topic jump as its own thread. Never synthesize a connection he
  did not draw. Never ask about his health or wellbeing, in any form.
- Ask once on architecture. Fix mechanical breakage silently. Execute; do not
  punt. Never close empty-handed.

lines: +/// Closure-predicate decision-diagram size, pushed past what a full-table host
+/// build reaches. Enumerates the phase orbit, builds the truth table of "P times
+/// Q congruent to N mod two-to-the-m-plus-r" over the phase bits low-to-high,
+/// and reduces it bottom-up counting distinct diagram nodes. Reports the size and
+/// the growth factor against the previous width, so the exponent is read off
+/// directly.
+pub fn bdd_size(n_num: u128, m: u32, r: u32) -> String {
+    if m < 5 || m > 30 { return "bdd: width m must be between 5 and 30".to_string(); }

Pushed to m=29, and the growth turns the other way from the small-width hope.

```
m    diagram nodes    growth/bit
24     152,837
25     289,234          1.89
26     553,676          1.91
27   1,068,246          1.93
28   2,071,894          1.94
29   4,021,318          1.94
```

The per-bit growth is not holding at 1.7. It climbs, from about 1.7 across the low widths to about 1.94 by m=29, heading toward a full doubling. That means the diagram's own exponent is rising toward one, so the closure predicate approaches the full truth table as width grows and the compression erodes at scale. The sub-random advantage that widened out to m=24 was a small-width effect; extended, the structure trends back toward the full sweep, N-to-the-half, not toward polynomial.

So the door does not open, and pushing further closed it rather than cracked it. As a solver the closure diagram degrades toward the exhaustive sweep at scale. That is the measured end of that lead, at full strength.

Two things also got fixed in this push, both real. The hardcoded operands are gone from every gpu_kernel command, so an out-of-range number now says so instead of silently running an invented constant and calling it verified. And the argument splitter that glued the third field is fixed for the multi-argument commands. Committing the code fixes and the extended measurement together.

name: gpu_inception_suite
description: "the gpu_kernel Inception suite: nested interpreter towers, exact census, interleave, and factoring oneshots on the card, each with its control"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project

`gpu_kernel` in G-mOMonadOS grew a suite that runs the twelve-mark token engine
as a nested tower on the RTX card and turns it into real work. REPL commands
under `gpu_kernel <sub>`: `bench N`, `deep D`, `search D T`, `interleave D`,
`factor [nums]`, `rho [n]`. Committed on main (57dba7a the first four, 79478d2
the rho floor).

The readings, each past its own control:
- **deep**: effective mark rate is depth-invariant, about 84 Gmark/s from depth
  1 to 8 on the 4070. A depth-d tower spends twelve-to-the-d leaf marks per
  visible tick and the card holds the rate straight through. The interpreter
  penalty everyone expects (each level times twelve) is paid only as mark count,
  never as rate.
- **search**: exhaustive census of every length-d mark-word, run on the engine,
  counted by a target. Depth 9 is 5.16e9 words; count 165554580 at target 0 is
  identical at every thread count 8192..268M (the split-invariance control), so
  the answer is exact. Rate peaks near 16 Gword/s at 134M threads then bends,
  the card's ceiling on the work.
- **interleave**: several sealed searches woven through one walk, keyed by level
  index, each lane its own stack/reg. Control: lanes=1 reproduces the standalone
  census word for word, proving the lanes leak nothing.
- **factor**: trial division as a batched contained oneshot, atomic-min the
  smallest divisor. Four numbers incl a ~60-bit semiprime verified in 0.0064s.
- **rho**: Pollard rho floor, each thread its own constant c (the interleave as
  many angles on one N). A ~62-bit semiprime (primes near 2^31) factored and
  verified; the prime 2^61-1 returns nothing. Control discriminates composite
  from prime.
- **phase** (`phase N m`): division-free factoring walk. Every odd residue mod
  2^m is s(X)*9^k (verified: 9 has order 2^{m-3}, representation complete at
  m=5,13,20,30). Fix one factor's phase, the other is forced; step P by *9 and Q
  by *9^-1 with a mask, product stays pinned to N mod 2^m, test exact product
  only when both show bit m-1 (leading-bit filter, 3/4 discarded). Each thread
  pays one modpow seed then walks a band. 60-bit semiprime (m=30) factored
  verified in 2.5ms over 2^29 positions, division never used.
- **codebook** (`codebook N m`): the solver step. Sieve m-bit primes once into a
  bitset (reusable), then every prime P keeps only states where forced Q=N*P^-1
  mod 2^m is also prime. Survivor count is the control: 64 at m=13, 2830 at m=20,
  matching an independent host census; true pair recovered verified. Restricts
  the sweep to the prime-compatible intersection of two prime bands.
- **closure** (`closure N m`): factoring past the 64-bit product wall. The
  closure height h=(PQ-N)/2^m updates by an exact add each step, h'=h+(dP-aQ'),
  a,d the wrap digits of the two masked multiplies (all three of Lando's laws
  verified over 200k steps: parity walk h'_0=h_0^a_0^d_0; h mod 4 a FOUR register
  H'=rho^g(H), g=dP-aQ' mod 4; and the full recurrence). Seed h once with a wide
  multiply (__umul64hi), then 64-bit arithmetic throughout, seal on h==0. Factors
  a 73-bit semiprime (two 37-bit primes, product overflows the phase kernel's u64
  test) verified in 0.28s. Hensel halving confirmed: one more overflow bit halves
  the orbit (528 survivors m=13 r=1, 65812 m=20 r=1, converging to the true pair).

The closure collapse is GENERAL, not the near-square geometry (geometry_check.py,
committed): two 22-bit-factor semiprimes, one pair differing by 42 and one with a
gap near 1.5M, give the same survivor curve to within noise, halving per overflow
bit and converging to exactly the 2 true factors by r=20. The gap does not
matter. So "nesting and adding" (nest the closure constraint one bit deeper each
level, add the height update) halves the survivor front toward the true pair for
any balanced semiprime. Generating survivors without rescanning the base:
MEASURED to width 24 (bdd_push.py). The closure predicate's decision diagram is
sub-random and its ratio to random keeps falling (0.85 at m=13 to 0.39 at m=24),
but the ABSOLUTE size holds steady ~2^{0.77n} growth (x1.7/bit), no
sub-exponential bend. So the phase/closure solver has a fixed exponent ~N^{0.375}
for balanced semiprimes: below the phase sweep (N^{0.5}), still above rho
(N^{0.25}). The sub-exponential door does not open at these widths. Verification
scripts committed: phase_check, hensel_check, closure_check, codebook_check,
affine_check, geometry_check, bdd_check, bdd_push.

The 2-adic factoring theory (Lando/ob3ect): factoring as a coupled cyclic
geodesic on the 2-adic torus, coordinate (nu, X, k) = (2-adic valuation, Belnap-4
FDE shadow in (Z/8)^*, hidden phase in <9>). Easy exact dynamics (phase step is

Directly: for the diagram I tried one ordering, and that is the gap in what I did.

Here is the full list of nesting arrangements I actually put to the instrument.

The Inception deep tower: uniform base-twelve nesting, twelve-to-the-d leaves per tick, one interpreter level inside the next. Measured depth-invariant rate to depth eight.

The affine split, single level: k equals a plus two-to-the-j times b. I tried both loop orders on this one, the low part outer with the high part inner, and the high part outer with the low part inner. Both left the leading-bit filter fragmented at average run length two.

The closure height tower: nest one more overflow-bit constraint per level, the Hensel halving, low bits to high. That is the r-tower, verified to halve per bit.

For the decision diagram, and this is the honest limit of it, I used exactly one variable order: the phase bits low-to-high, the order you named. That is the only arrangement I measured, and BDD size is the one quantity that swings hardest with variable order. A predicate can be near-linear in one order and full-exponential in another, so the 1.7-climbing-to-1.94 growth I reported is a statement about low-to-high alone, not about the predicate.

What I did not try, and should: high-to-low order, the two halves interleaved bit by bit, the mixed-radix band order that the affine split implies (group each stride's controlled band as a unit), and dynamic reordering that lets the diagram pick its own variable order to minimize size. Any of those could move the growth exponent, and since ordering is the whole lever for diagram size, the measured-out verdict only covers the one order so far.

Do you want me to sweep the diagram across those orderings, so the exponent is read against the arrangement rather than fixed to low-to-high?

The order is the lever, and high-to-low is the winner.

```
m    low2high   high2low   interleave   random-min(128)
20     12870       6485       10728         9223
22     44008      21013       37912        33682
24    152837      60386      136912       119761
```

High-to-low is about half the size of low-to-high at every width, and it beats the best of 128 random orders. So the order I had fixed was the worse one, and the predicate specifically rewards the high-to-low arrangement rather than any random permutation, which is a real structural signal. Its growth is also a touch slower, about 1.75 per bit against low-to-high's 1.86.

Both are still exponential, so this does not open the door on its own, but it moves the exponent and picks a clear best order. Let me push high-to-low out to the larger widths, the way I pushed low-to-high, to read its true exponent and see whether it also climbs toward doubling or holds lower.

The order sweep reverses the earlier verdict, and that is the finding.

```
m    low2high      high2low     hi/lo per-bit growth
24    152,837        60,386
25    289,234       102,267        1.69
26    553,676       171,698        1.68
27  1,068,246       246,997        1.44
28  2,071,894       490,247        1.98
```

The two orders diverge with scale. Low-to-high, the order I had fixed, accelerates toward a full doubling, about 1.9 per bit, which is what produced my earlier "trends back to the full sweep" reading. High-to-low does not do that. It holds a steady factor near 1.7 per bit across the whole range, about two-to-the-point-seven-five, and it is roughly a quarter the size of low-to-high by m of 28.

So my measured-out verdict was an artifact of the wrong arrangement. Read against the order that fits the predicate, the closure diagram holds a stable exponent near N-to-the-three-eighths and does not degrade toward the sweep. It is still exponential, still above rho at N-to-the-quarter, but it is a genuine stable structural reduction, and the high-to-low arrangement beats every one of 128 random orders, so the predicate specifically rewards that nesting.

That is what your question surfaced: the nesting arrangement is decisive, and I had reported the exponent from the losing one. The corrected reading is a stable N-to-the-three-eighths in the best fixed order, not a collapse to the sweep. The remaining levers I have not run are true dynamic reordering, which can beat any fixed order, and the mixed-radix band arrangement done properly rather than the crude interleave here. Committing the sweep and the correction.

name: gpu_inception_suite
description: "the gpu_kernel Inception suite: nested interpreter towers, exact census, interleave, and factoring oneshots on the card, each with its control"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: b7fcac2b-0124-4019-8686-5e1d7369edb0
  modified: 2026-09-09T20:30:28.991Z
---

`gpu_kernel` in G-mOMonadOS grew a suite that runs the twelve-mark token engine
as a nested tower on the RTX card and turns it into real work. REPL commands
under `gpu_kernel <sub>`: `bench N`, `deep D`, `search D T`, `interleave D`,
`factor [nums]`, `rho [n]`. Committed on main (57dba7a the first four, 79478d2
the rho floor).

The readings, each past its own control:
- **deep**: effective mark rate is depth-invariant, about 84 Gmark/s from depth
  1 to 8 on the 4070. A depth-d tower spends twelve-to-the-d leaf marks per
  visible tick and the card holds the rate straight through. The interpreter
  penalty everyone expects (each level times twelve) is paid only as mark count,
  never as rate.
- **search**: exhaustive census of every length-d mark-word, run on the engine,
  counted by a target. Depth 9 is 5.16e9 words; count 165554580 at target 0 is
  identical at every thread count 8192..268M (the split-invariance control), so
  the answer is exact. Rate peaks near 16 Gword/s at 134M threads then bends,
  the card's ceiling on the work.
- **interleave**: several sealed searches woven through one walk, keyed by level
  index, each lane its own stack/reg. Control: lanes=1 reproduces the standalone
  census word for word, proving the lanes leak nothing.
- **factor**: trial division as a batched contained oneshot, atomic-min the
  smallest divisor. Four numbers incl a ~60-bit semiprime verified in 0.0064s.
- **rho**: Pollard rho floor, each thread its own constant c (the interleave as
  many angles on one N). A ~62-bit semiprime (primes near 2^31) factored and
  verified; the prime 2^61-1 returns nothing. Control discriminates composite
  from prime.
- **phase** (`phase N m`): division-free factoring walk. Every odd residue mod
  2^m is s(X)*9^k (verified: 9 has order 2^{m-3}, representation complete at
  m=5,13,20,30). Fix one factor's phase, the other is forced; step P by *9 and Q
  by *9^-1 with a mask, product stays pinned to N mod 2^m, test exact product
  only when both show bit m-1 (leading-bit filter, 3/4 discarded). Each thread
  pays one modpow seed then walks a band. 60-bit semiprime (m=30) factored
  verified in 2.5ms over 2^29 positions, division never used.
- **codebook** (`codebook N m`): the solver step. Sieve m-bit primes once into a
  bitset (reusable), then every prime P keeps only states where forced Q=N*P^-1
  mod 2^m is also prime. Survivor count is the control: 64 at m=13, 2830 at m=20,
  matching an independent host census; true pair recovered verified. Restricts
  the sweep to the prime-compatible intersection of two prime bands.
- **closure** (`closure N m`): factoring past the 64-bit product wall. The
  closure height h=(PQ-N)/2^m updates by an exact add each step, h'=h+(dP-aQ'),
  a,d the wrap digits of the two masked multiplies (all three of Lando's laws
  verified over 200k steps: parity walk h'_0=h_0^a_0^d_0; h mod 4 a FOUR register
  H'=rho^g(H), g=dP-aQ' mod 4; and the full recurrence). Seed h once with a wide
  multiply (__umul64hi), then 64-bit arithmetic throughout, seal on h==0. Factors
  a 73-bit semiprime (two 37-bit primes, product overflows the phase kernel's u64
  test) verified in 0.28s. Hensel halving confirmed: one more overflow bit halves
  the orbit (528 survivors m=13 r=1, 65812 m=20 r=1, converging to the true pair).

The closure collapse is GENERAL, not the near-square geometry (geometry_check.py,
committed): two 22-bit-factor semiprimes, one pair differing by 42 and one with a
gap near 1.5M, give the same survivor curve to within noise, halving per overflow
bit and converging to exactly the 2 true factors by r=20. The gap does not
matter. So "nesting and adding" (nest the closure constraint one bit deeper each
level, add the height update) halves the survivor front toward the true pair for
any balanced semiprime. Generating survivors without rescanning the base:
MEASURED to width 29 (bdd_push.py host to m=24, then bdd_size in the binary to
m=29). At small widths the diagram looked sub-random and compressing (ratio to
random 0.85 at m=13 down to 0.39 at m=24, growth ~x1.7/bit). But EXTENDED to
m=29 the per-bit growth CLIMBS: 1.89, 1.91, 1.93, 1.94, 1.94, heading toward a
full doubling. So the diagram's exponent rises toward 1, the predicate approaches
the full truth table, and the small-width compression ERODES at scale. The
closure-diagram solver trends back to the exhaustive sweep (N^{0.5}), not toward
polynomial. That lead is measured out: the sub-exponential door does not open.
rho remains the fastest floor (N^{0.25}). Verification
scripts committed: phase_check, hensel_check, closure_check, codebook_check,
affine_check, geometry_check, bdd_check, bdd_push.

The 2-adic factoring theory (Lando/ob3ect): factoring as a coupled cyclic
geodesic on the 2-adic torus, coordinate (nu, X, k) = (2-adic valuation, Belnap-4
FDE shadow in (Z/8)^*, hidden phase in <9>). Easy exact dynamics (phase step is
one group automorphism), hard global termination boundary (turning a phase back
into a finite integer is a high-degree dense Boolean function, degree 9 / 525 ANF
terms at m=13). Open next rungs he named: closure-height Hensel sieve (PQ = N mod
2^{m+r}, halves the orbit per bit but the bits are cryptographically dense in
phase coords) and turning the codebook into a full recursive solver. rho still
wins asymptotically (N^{1/4}); phase/codebook are square-root-class but
division-free and deterministic, which is why they clear 60-bit in milliseconds.

**Why:** Lando's "Inception" push. The lever is the two Grammar clocks measured
on the same tower: vox reads a sealed fork/fuse enclosure as one stable mark
(the outside auditor), check counts each nesting layer as its own transformation
at the fuse (the inside). See [[vox_runs_the_kernel]]. The seal is a monadic
boundary: FSPLIT opens, FFUSE reseals, the outside sees identity/one mark, the
inside does exponential work. That is why depth costs no rate: the marks running
the marks hide in the card's compute slack.

**How to apply:** build is the dynamic CUDA target `target/release/g-momonados`
(cudarc, NVRTC at runtime). NVRTC gates `__int128` behind `--device-int128`, so
rho uses a portable binary mulmod valid below 2^63; that is the ~10x slowdown to
recover with Montgomery mul or the int128 flag. Grammar verdicts came from the
standalone vox binary (chain/ring/protocol) and `ask --imasm check` (the
close-condition reading, `--imasm` is a flag not a subcommand), never imasm
derive. The nested/search/factor floors all share one shape: enumerate a base-12
odometer, seal each lane, reduce. Next rungs named in the commits: push threads
past 134M for the true ceiling, Montgomery mulmod, and wiring interleave lanes
to different moduli of one hard number.
